clinicalPearls: A rare, progressive, and fatal encephalitis caused by persistence of a defective measles virus in the brain, typically developing years after the initial measles infection
The risk is greatest when natural measles is acquired in infancy, and the latent interval before SSPE is often 6 to 10 years or more
It evolves through recognisable stages, beginning with subtle cognitive and behavioural change and declining school performance
The hallmark second stage is periodic myoclonic jerks, followed by progressive dementia, spasticity, rigidity, and eventually a vegetative state
The electroencephalogram characteristically shows periodic complexes that coincide with the myoclonic jerks
Cerebrospinal fluid reveals markedly raised measles-specific antibody with oligoclonal bands and evidence of intrathecal antibody synthesis, with normal or mildly raised protein
There is no curative therapy; agents such as interferon and isoprinosine have been tried with limited benefit, and prevention through measles immunisation is paramount
reference.pathophysiology: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis results from persistence of the measles virus in neurones and glia after apparently complete recovery from acute measles. Over the ensuing years the virus accumulates mutations, particularly affecting the matrix and other envelope genes, so that it can no longer produce complete infectious particles but continues to spread cell to cell within the brain. This defective, persistent infection provokes a chronic inflammatory and immune response, with intense intrathecal production of anti-measles antibody, alongside slowly progressive destruction of both grey and white matter, hence the term panencephalitis. Neurones and oligodendrocytes contain viral inclusions, and there is perivascular inflammation, gliosis, and demyelination. The relentless accumulation of neuronal loss underlies the stepwise clinical deterioration from cognitive decline through myoclonus to a vegetative state and death.
additionalDifferentials: Neurodegenerative disorders and leukodystrophies of childhood and adolescence
Inborn errors of metabolism presenting with regression
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and other prion disorders
additionalInvestigations: Electroencephalography demonstrating periodic complexes synchronous with myoclonus
Cerebrospinal fluid measles antibody titre with paired serum for antibody index and oligoclonal bands
MRI of the brain showing white-matter change and later cerebral atrophy
Detailed history of prior measles infection, especially in infancy, and immunisation status
Molecular detection of measles virus RNA in brain tissue in atypical cases
Exclusion of metabolic, prion, and autoimmune causes of progressive encephalopathy
redFlags: Progressive cognitive decline with new periodic myoclonic jerks in a child or adolescent
Rapid neurological deterioration into rigidity or a vegetative state
Loss of safe swallowing and airway protection
Intractable seizures or autonomic instability in advanced disease
reference.prognosis: SSPE is usually relentlessly progressive and fatal, most patients dying within a few years of onset; occasional cases follow a more prolonged or fluctuating course, but spontaneous long-term remission is rare and no treatment reliably arrests it.
pitfalls: Dismissing early behavioural and academic decline as a psychological or educational problem
Not recognising the diagnostic value of periodic EEG complexes coinciding with myoclonus
Relying on serum measles antibody alone rather than demonstrating intrathecal antibody synthesis
Underestimating the importance of measles vaccination in prevention, especially where infants are infected
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
